rationale: Step 7 is the specific mechanism that operationalizes the recurring cycle, making it concrete: iterate per business process and react to workflow changes.
Analytics provides the feedback data (telemetry, baselines, deviation alerts) that turns the cycle from a linear sequence into a genuinely closed loop.
Analytics supplies the monitoring and behavioral-baseline data that enables the lower-tempo policy refinement called for in Step 7.
The hybrid model is the reason the cycle is indefinite — you never finish because ZT and perimeter workflows coexist permanently.
Dual-mode infrastructure (ID mgmt, device mgmt, logging) is the concrete set of requirements that the indefinite hybrid imposes on common systems.
Dual-mode requirements only exist because the hybrid model is indefinite — without indefinite coexistence, infrastructure wouldn't need to serve both modes.
Since pure greenfield is rarely viable, the hybrid model is not a temporary concession but the expected and necessary migration path.
Both claims converge on the same strategic conclusion: organizations should not expect or pursue greenfield, instead evolving what they already have.
The prevalence of legacy implicit-trust systems is the structural reason greenfield is rarely viable for existing organizations.
Brownfield's 3–4× timeline (due to recursive device re-profiling) provides the quantitative justification for not rushing past monitor mode.
The steep brownfield cost reinforces why greenfield would be preferable, but since greenfield is rarely viable, brownfield reality must be planned for.
The foundational inventory prerequisite is presented as the solution to the chicken-and-egg barrier — you must build inventories despite not yet having migrated.
Step 1 (identify all subjects) operationalizes the actor-inventory portion of the foundational prerequisite.
Step 2 (catalog all assets) operationalizes the asset-inventory portion of the foundational prerequisite.
Step 2 follows Step 1 in the NIST 7-step cycle — asset cataloging builds on the subject identification that precedes it.
You cannot select which business process to migrate first (Step 3) until you have catalogued the assets and subjects involved (Steps 1–2).
Policy formulation (Step 4) requires a specific candidate business process to be selected first (Step 3) so that asset value, risk, and upstream/downstream resources can be evaluated.
Choosing a ZT solution (Step 5) depends on the access criteria and trust-evaluation approach (criteria-based vs. score-based) decided during policy formulation (Step 4).
You cannot deploy in reporting-only mode (Step 6) until a candidate solution has been selected (Step 5).
Reporting-only mode is the NIST 7-step framing of the log phase in the log-then-enforce pattern independently validated by Google and PagerDuty.
Rushing past monitor mode is the specific mistake that undermines the reporting-only deployment step, skipping the essential data-collection baseline.
The log-then-enforce pattern, validated by two independent case studies, provides the empirical evidence for why rushing past monitor mode is the biggest mistake.
Legacy implicit-trust systems create the interoperability gap that ZT proxies (forward and reverse) are designed to bridge.
ZT proxies are one concrete mechanism that enables dual-mode infrastructure, allowing non-ZT-aware legacy components to coexist with ZT services during the indefinite hybrid period.
The NSA's identification of organizational commitment as the primary challenge explains why roadblocks like political resistance and IAM immaturity persist and are surmountable only with buy-in.
Blending top-down strategic vision with bottom-up tactical execution is the practical method for building the enterprise-wide organizational commitment that the NSA identifies as critical.
The 3-phase VPN→RBAC→branch-removal case study exemplifies blended execution: top-down vision (ZT architecture) paired with bottom-up tactical steps (VPN replacement for 1,000 users).
Incomplete enterprise knowledge is one of the documented, predictable roadblocks — specifically the resource-visibility-gap and analysis-paralysis categories.
The 3-phase adoption path (VPN replacement → RBAC → branch removal) is a concrete, real-world case study that instantiates the incremental recurring cycle.
Starting with VPN replacement for 1,000 users is a low-risk cloud/remote-worker workflow — exactly the starting point NIST's Step 3 recommends.
Using existing Chef deployment to generate per-host iptables microsegmentation is a concrete example of ZT as an evolution of existing capabilities, not a greenfield rip-and-replace.
The five-pillar segmentation methodology (VLAN→Firewall→dACLs→TrustSec) operationalizes the policy-formulation step by providing a concrete enforcement hierarchy for identity-driven access decisions.
Both advocate iterative refinement starting from existing infrastructure — segmentation starts with 5–7 broad enclaves, just as config management leverages already-deployed tools.
The C2S/S2S distinction refines Step 3 by clarifying that the 'low-risk' starting-point recommendation favors client-to-server for most organizations, while server-to-server requires DevOps maturity.
Different migration starting points imply different solution criteria — a C2S migration evaluates client footprint and BYOD, while S2S migration prioritizes east-west traffic patterns.
The monitoring data collected during reporting-only mode (traffic patterns, access baselines, behavioral norms) is the raw material that analytics consumes to close the loop.
Migrating one business process at a time (Step 3) is the mechanism that makes indefinite ZT/perimeter coexistence operationally feasible.
Expanding ZTA to additional business processes (Step 7) requires policy to be formulated for each new candidate, making Step 4 a recurring dependency of Step 7.
